title: Pursuit of supermarkets sees ACCC wade into politics
full_text:
Competition The watchdog has pursued Coles and Woolworths with vigour, perpetuating a political narrative that those companies are greedy and ripping off consumers.
In its own words, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission's role is to "administer and enforce the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 and other legislation, promoting competition, fair trading and regulating national infrastructure for the benefit of all Australians".
The object of the CCA is to "enhance the welfare of Australians through the promotion of competition and fair trading and provision for consumer protection". It would be to the benefit of all Australians for the ACCC to remember its purpose.
Over recent weeks, much has been said about how the government's proposed tax changes will decrease the international competitiveness of the Australian economy as a place to invest.
But due in large part to regulatory overreach, obstruction and selective heavy-handedness, Australia was not a particularly investable place to begin with.
When investing anywhere, public companies need to be sure that, within the bounds of applicable laws and regulations, they remain free to pursue their core objective of generating shareholder returns.
This is not an argument against regulation. Regulation sets the rules of the game.
Its consistent enforcement enables commercial decisions to be made. Properly enforced and with regard to its purpose, regulation can be a competitive advantage for a market. Done poorly, enforcement can also deter investment.
Unfortunately, competition and consumer regulation in Australia increasingly appears to be moving towards the latter.
At a potentially high long-term cost to everyday Australians, the ACCC seems to be adopting an approach more politically or ideologically aligned than should be tolerated of an independent regulator, and more averse than it should be to shareholder returns and natural market forces.
Few examples are needed. Perhaps the most obvious is the ACCC's approach to the big supermarkets.
Not much can be said of matters still before a court, though Justice Michael O'Bryan's question of whether consumers were harmed by Coles' conduct in its "Down Down" promotion, which he found to be misleading, is noteworthy.
Outside the courts, the ACCC has for several years pursued Coles and Woolworths, as well as wholesaler Metcash, with vigour, perpetuating a political narrative that those companies are greedy and ripping off Australian consumers.
The mundane findings of its own inquiry into the sector appear to have been no barrier to this continuing; it seems rather too happy a coincidence that the ACCC's first decision to oppose an acquisition under the new merger regime happened to involve Coles.
Although said to arise from preserving competition from smaller independents, the benefits to consumers of the decision to block Coles from opening a second store in Kalgoorlie are not immediately obvious.
Conversely, the costs to Coles' shareholders, who presumably include many Kalgoorlie residents through their super accounts, are clear.
If it is impermissible for Coles to expand in an area it has assessed as likely to be profitable, growth for shareholders can come only from raising prices or cutting costs - both options that appear to be automatically looked on unfavourably by the ACCC when adopted by large companies.
That is one of the broader difficulties at play. Competition law is not meant to punish profit, scalability or success. Its concern is whether conduct harms the competitive process and, ultimately, consumer welfare. A regulator may properly ask whether consumers are being misled or excluded. It should be slower to treat the pursuit of profit as evidence of wrongdoing. Given the ACCC's ardent defence of competition in such matters, the speed with which that defence appears to soften when words such as climate or sustainability are raised is striking.
Whatever one's views on climate politics, the institutional issue is the same. The ACCC is not an environmental regulator. It is a competition and consumer regulator. Its task is not to determine the pace or design of an energy transition, but to apply the statutory framework it is charged with enforcing.
In 2023, notwithstanding that it was not satisfied that Brookfield's proposed acquisition of Origin Energy would not be likely to substantially lessen competition, the ACCC approved the ultimately unsuccessful transaction because the public benefits were said to outweigh the detriments.
The benefits identified were an acceleration of the rollout of renewable energy generation and more rapid reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, though no analysis or explanation of why either would be a public benefit was provided. That point, despite being highly contested, was simply taken as true.
More recently, the ACCC released a guide to "Sustainability collaborations and Australian competition law", which is premised on unsubstantiated claims that "environmental harm, including climate change, pollution and biodiversity loss, represents a special category of threat to the environment and the economy".
Again, the point does not appear to have been interrogated through the lens required by the regulator; it is just accepted.
In the context of competition regulation, the terms "public benefit" and "public detriment" are applied broadly.
Although precise quantification is not required, any claimed benefits (or detriments) should be based on commercially realistic estimates and founded on the economic principles of efficiency and total welfare.
Whether this is how climate and sustainability goals have been considered by the ACCC is far from clear.
The ACCC does not exist to promote any political agenda. Nor does it exist to promote the generation of shareholder returns. It exists to enhance the welfare of Australians through the promotion of competition, fair trading and consumer protection.
By wading so obviously into political matters (the above being just a few examples), the ACCC risks undermining its independence and depriving companies of the certainty they need to invest in Australia.
If the enforcement of competition regulation is dictated by the political objectives of the day, there can be no long-term certainty about what is and is not allowed, and thus no long-term commercial decision-making. The jurisdiction simply becomes uninvestable.
If the ACCC continues down its current path, international investment in Australia may further diminish and the growth of Australian companies may stall.
That would be to the economic detriment of all Australians, and contrary to one of the very purposes for which the ACCC exists.
Stephanie Derrington is an investing analyst at Allan Gray and previously a commercial litigator. Disclosure: Allan Gray Australia owns shares in Woolworths and Metcash, and in other ASX-listed companies that have been or are currently subject to ACCC investigations and enforcement action.
